symbols.name: input sequence
symbols.meaning: The sequence of ring elements $x_0$ through $x_{2r-1}$ to which the transform is applied.
symbols.quote: For a sequence $x_0,\dots,x_{2r-1}$ of ring elements, let $t$ be the input position and $s$ the frequency index, $s=0,\dots,2r-1$.

symbols.name: input position
symbols.meaning: The index of an input entry, running from 0 to $2r-1$.
symbols.quote: For a sequence $x_0,\dots,x_{2r-1}$ of ring elements, let $t$ be the input position and $s$ the frequency index, $s=0,\dots,2r-1$.

symbols.name: frequency index
symbols.meaning: The index of an output frequency, running from 0 to $2r-1$.
symbols.quote: For a sequence $x_0,\dots,x_{2r-1}$ of ring elements, let $t$ be the input position and $s$ the frequency index, $s=0,\dots,2r-1$.

symbols.name: half-transform index
symbols.meaning: The index, running from 0 to $r-1$, that labels the even outputs $\hat x_{2i}$ and the odd outputs $\hat x_{2i+1}$.
symbols.quote: Since $y^{s(t+r)}=(-1)^s y^{st}$, for $i=0,\dots,r-1$ we get $\hat x_{2i}=\sum_{t<r} y^{2it}(x_t+x_{t+r})$ and $\hat x_{2i+1}=\sum_{t<r} y^{2it}\,y^t(x_t-x_{t+r})$.

symbols.name: second sequence
symbols.meaning: A second sequence of ring elements, transformed by the same rule as $x$.
symbols.quote: Let $z$ be a second sequence of ring elements, transformed the same way.

symbols.name: position in z
symbols.meaning: The index of an entry of $z$, summed over together with $t$.
symbols.quote: Expanding, $\hat x_s\hat z_s=\sum_{t,q} y^{s(t+q)}x_tz_q$, where $q$ is a position in $z$.

symbols.name: convolution position
symbols.meaning: The output position of the cyclic convolution $x\ast z$, taken modulo $2r$.
symbols.quote: Since $y^{2r}=1$, the exponent depends only on $h\equiv t+q \pmod{2r}$, so $\hat x_s\hat z_s=\sum_h y^{sh}(x\ast z)_h$, where $(x\ast z)_h=\sum_{t+q\equiv h \pmod{2r}} x_tz_q$ is the cyclic convolution with output position $h$.

relations.quote: It works in the [polynomial ring modulo yʳ + 1](polynomial-ring-y.md).
It is built on $y$ as a [primitive root of unity](roots-of-unity.md) of order $2r$: $y^r=-1$, so $y^{2r}=1$, and no smaller positive power of $y$ equals $1$.
A synthetic polynomial transform generalizes the [discrete Fourier transform](fourier-transform.md) to a polynomial ring whose roots of unity are powers of $y$.
